task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper explainer for general readers answering the question: What are superconductors, and why does the quest for a room-temperature superconductor matter so much? Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of February 12, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: Superconductors have zero electrical resistance under suitable conditions below a critical temperature, allowing a steady current to flow without resistive heating.
Conventional electrical conductors such as copper dissipate energy as heat. The power lost to electrical resistance equals current squared multiplied by resistance.
In a superconductor, electrons form bound pairs (Cooper pairs) that travel through the material's lattice without scattering off atoms, the mechanism that causes resistance in normal conductors.
Established superconductors that work at ordinary pressure require cooling below room temperature; most conventional superconductors work only near absolute zero (minus 273 degrees Celsius).

High-temperature superconductors — a class discovered in the 1980s — work at temperatures achievable with liquid nitrogen (minus 196 degrees Celsius), which is far cheaper than liquid helium used for conventional superconductors.

Physicist Dr. Elena Saito of Lakeside Materials Institute said: "Room temperature superconductivity would be one of the most transformative material discoveries in history. Every motor, every transformer, every power line would work on a different physics."

A claimed room-temperature, high-pressure superconductor published in 2023 by a research group attracted intense scrutiny; follow-up attempts by other laboratories failed to reproduce the results, and the paper was retracted.
The reproducibility crisis in superconductor research has been a recurring problem; several high-profile room-temperature claims since 2015 have failed independent verification.
Current applications of superconductors include MRI machine magnets, particle accelerator magnets, maglev train levitation systems, and laboratory scientific instruments.
High-temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets are used in compact fusion reactors being developed by private companies; their stronger field strength allows smaller tokamak designs.
Superconducting power cables are being piloted in urban grids in Germany and South Korea, carrying 5 times more current than conventional cables of the same diameter with lower losses.

A room-temperature superconductor that worked at atmospheric pressure would enable superconducting electronics, low-loss power transmission, faster trains, and dramatically more powerful medical and scientific magnets.

Dr. Saito said the theoretical understanding of high-temperature superconductivity is still incomplete; the mechanism that allows some materials to superconduct at liquid nitrogen temperatures is not fully explained.
Manufacturing superconducting wire is technically challenging; the ceramic materials that superconduct at higher temperatures are brittle and difficult to form into flexible cables.
The global superconductor market is valued at approximately $8 billion per year, dominated by medical imaging and scientific applications.

Quantum computing systems use superconducting circuits cooled near absolute zero as quantum bits (qubits); companies including Google and IBM rely on superconducting technology for their current quantum computers.

Dr. Saito said the field has genuine theoretical reasons to believe room-temperature superconductivity is physically possible; the challenge is finding the right material, which may require systematic exploration of millions of compounds.

High-entropy alloys and hydrogen-rich materials called hydrides are current areas of intense research; some hydrides superconduct at high temperature but only under enormous pressures that preclude practical use.
If achieved and scalable, room-temperature superconducting transmission lines could reduce global electricity losses by hundreds of terawatt-hours annually.

The National Science Foundation has increased funding for superconductor material discovery research following the failed room-temperature claim in 2023, which the NSF said highlighted both the potential importance and the need for rigorous verification protocols.
